Natural underground cavities are hypogean spaces 
formed through natural processes, encompassing 
their environment, mineral and water content, the 
host rock body in which they are embedded, and the 
fauna and flora present. These are commonly known 
as caves, grottos, dens, abysses, furnas, or holes. The 
term “speleological heritage” refers to the set of biotic 
and abiotic elements, whether subterranean or surface, 
represented by natural underground cavities or those 
associated with them. Therefore, speleological heritage 
has a multidisciplinary nature, including biodiversity, 
geodiversity, sociocultural diversity, and attributes 
related to hydrology, scenics qualities, historical and 
cultural significance, socioeconomic factors, as well as 
paleontological and archaeological aspects associated 
with caves.
Brazil is a country of continental dimensions with 
significant geological, biological, and cultural diversity, 
which is also reflected in its speleological heritage. 
The Brazilian territory features geographic, geological, 
and climatic characteristics that favor the formation 
of caves, in addition to extensive areas conducive to 
their occurrence. Data from 2022 indicate that Brazil 
has 23,378 registered natural underground cavities 
in the National Register of Speleological Information 
(Canie), with a potential of over 300,000 caves. The 
country exhibits high diversity in cave types, formed 
in carbonate rocks (limestone, marble, and dolomite), 
siliciclastic rocks (quartzite and sandstone), ferruginous 
formations (banded iron formations and canga), 
granitic rocks, and volcanic rocks, distributed across 
nearly the entire national territory. Brazil also possesses 
a rich subterranean biodiversity, with numerous 
species of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, 
and terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates that utilize 
the underground environment either temporarily, 
permanently, or exclusively (troglobites). Additionally, 
cultural diversity is evidenced in various caves through 
rock art and archaeological artifacts from peoples of 
different ethnicities.
In addition to the great diversity present in Brazilian 
caves, they also exhibit attributes that demonstrate their 
scientific, cultural, social, and economic importance. 
Several cave-dwelling species participate in the 
formation (genesis) of caves or perform vital ecological 
functions such as controlling insects (pests), seed 
dispersal, pollination, or maintaining cave ecosystems 
through food resources. Therefore, these species are 
crucial for maintaining the balance of both internal and 
external environments. Microorganisms found in caves 
possess pharmaceutical and biotechnological potential 
to produce antibiotics, effluent treatment, promotion 
of plant growth, control of plant pathogens, metal 
biotransformation, and soil remediation. Caves serve 
as sites for fossil deposition, which are essential for 
taxonomic, anatomical, and paleoecological knowledge 
regarding vertebrates that inhabited Brazil during the 
Pleistocene. Artifacts and archaeological records are 
fundamental for understanding the process of human 
occupation in the country. Additionally, caves contribute 
to paleoclimatology by providing insights into climate 
changes over time. Many Brazilian caves are used 
for regulated tourism and environmental education 
practices, fostering awareness about the importance 
of Brazil’s speleological heritage and its preservation. 
Regulated tourism also provides a significant source of 
income for local communities, who can act as guides, 
service providers, or engage in the commercialization 
of local and artisanal products. Therefore, given the 
importance and diversity of the speleological heritage, 
the protection and conservation of this rich and unique 
environment are both necessary and urgent.
In 2009, the Ministry of the Environment issued 
Ordinance nº 358, establishing the Programa Nacional 
de Conservação do Patrimônio Espeleológico (PNCPE). 
The PNCPE aims to develop a national strategy for the 
conservation and sustainable use of Brazil’s speleological 
heritage through the formulation, monitoring, and 
implementation of conservation actions. The Centro 
Nacional de Pesquisa e Conservação de Cavernas 
(ICMBio/Cecav) is responsible for developing Action 
Plans for the conservation of Brazil’s speleological 
heritage. In 2011, ICMBio/Cecav, in collaboration with 
various partners, developed the National Action Plan for 
the Conservation of Speleological Heritage in the Karst 
Areas of the São Francisco River Basin (Cavernas do São 
Francisco NAP). This NAP concluded its cycle in 2017 
and achieved significant milestones for the conservation 
of speleological heritage, both within the São Francisco 
River Basin’s Karst Areas and nationally. Consequently, 
the opportunity arose to develop a nationally 
comprehensive NAP, culminating in the creation of the 
National Action Plan for the Conservation of Brazil’s 
Speleological Heritage (Cavernas do Brasil NAP).

NAP Coverage Area
The Cavernas do Brasil NAP has a nationwide scope, with most of its actions also concentrated within this 
framework, primarily focusing on states and areas with the highest occurrence of caves. However, some initiatives 
aim to establish priority areas for implementing actions related to the prospecting, inventory, and conservation 
of speleological heritage.
Fotos: Ciro Albano; Fabio Nunes; Cláudia Brasileiro.

Occurrence in Protected Areas
The National System of Protected Areas (SNUC) aims to protect significant geological, geomorphological, 
speleological, archaeological, paleontological, and cultural features, as well as to safeguard threatened species. 
Consequently, some conservation units have been established with the objective of protecting Brazil’s speleological 
heritage (see examples below).
According to the National Registry of Protected Areas (December 2022), Brazil has 2,902 protected areas 
(PAs) at the federal, state, or municipal levels. Only 249 PAs (8.6%) have recorded caves within their boundaries, 
according to the Brazilian Speleological Heritage Statistical Yearbook (2022). These units host 7,750 caves (33%) 
registered in the National Speleological Information Database (CANIE), with 56% (4,368) located within sustainable 
use PAs and 44% (3,382) within full protection PAs. Approximately 59% (4,607) of these caves are within federal 
PAs, 37% (2,839) within state PAs, and 4% (304) within municipal PAs. Only 57 PAs have records of threatened 
cave species. Of the 169 threatened species included in the NAP, 96 (57%) have been recorded within federal, 
state, and/or municipal conservation units. The number of threatened species registered within protected areas,

Threats
Speleological 
heritage 
possesses 
unique 
geological, 
biological, 
and 
hydrological 
characteristics, characterized by 
high complexity and significant 
environmental 
fragility. 
These 
features are expressed both within 
the caves and in the external 
environment. The subterranean 
environment 
exhibits 
notable 
faunal endemism, low species 
abundance, striking scenic beauty, a 
diversity of morphological features, 
mineral deposits of various shapes 
(speleothems), and strategic water 
reservoirs. The cave environment is 
highly vulnerable to environmental 
changes that can disrupt and 
compromise 
its 
conservation 
status. 
Harmful 
environmental 
alterations can occur both inside 
the caves and in their influence 
zones, which include biotic and 
abiotic 
elements—surface 
and 
subterranean—that are essential 
for maintaining ecological balance 
and the physical integrity of the 
cave environment.
The rapid growth of the human 
population and the consequent 
expansion of economic activities 
have 
led 
to 
an 
exponential 
increase in pressure on natural 
resources. As a result, Brazil’s 
speleological 
heritage 
faces 
serious 
environmental 
threats 
stemming from socio-economic 
conflicts caused by activities or 
developments that utilize land 
and subsoil. The main threats to 
the national speleological heritage 
include: 
mining, 
deforestation, 
use 
of 
agrochemicals, 
illegal 
water 
extraction, 
wildfires, 
unplanned 
urban 
expansion, 
engineering works, hydroelectric 
dam construction, disorganized 
religious and tourism activities 
within caves, and vandalism. These 
activities 
can 
induce 
physical 
and hydrological changes in the 
subterranean environment and its 
influence zone, such as erosion, soil 
compaction, water contamination, 
alterations in hydrodynamics, slow 
subsidence or land collapse, and 
cave destruction, degradation, or 
obliteration. 
Unregulated 
cave 
visitation has led to vandalism 
and other damaging practices, 
such 
as 
speleotem 
breakage 
and theft, graffiti, and littering. 
Such 
alterations 
threaten 
the 
environmental stability and the 
physical and biological dynamics 
of the subterranean environment, 
potentially 
causing 
significant 
physical changes, habitat loss, 
and the local extinction of cave-
dwelling species.
In Brazil, of the estimated 
300,000 caves, fewer than 10% 
have been officially registered to 
date, and only about 10% of these 
have some form of fauna sampling. 
Most biological studies conducted 
in Brazilian caves are related 
to inventories, and only a small 
fraction of the recorded species 
are well understood ecologically. 
Given the large number of yet-
to-be-discovered 
caves, 
the 
high levels of endemism, and 
the low abundance of organisms 
inhabiting 
the 
subterranean 
environment, there remains a 
significant number of cave species 
to be documented and studied 
in Brazil. Therefore, investing in 
research and conservation of these 
environments is crucial to prevent 
the extinction of these species.

Strategy for the Conservation of Brazilian 
Speleological Heritage
The National Program for the Conservation 
of Threatened Species (Pró-Espécies), established 
by Ordinance nº 43/2014 of the Ministry of the 
Environment, sets forth the National Action Plans for the 
Conservation of Threatened Species (NAP). The primary 
purpose of the NAPs is to define actions aimed at the 
conservation and recovery of fauna species at risk of 
extinction. Additionally, Normative Instruction ICMBio 
nº 21/2018 provides guidelines for the development 
and implementation of these plans. NAPs are developed 
considering the main pressure vectors affecting the target 
species or environments and include objectives and 
actions established within a defined temporal horizon, 
with the goal of reversing or mitigating these threats.
The NAPs are prepared and implemented through a 
participatory process involving society, typically engaging 
specialists, public managers, organized civil society, 
representatives of productive sectors, and traditional 
communities, among other relevant stakeholders. This 
planning and management instrument has the potential 
to foster coordination among key social actors, as 
well as to guide the allocation of human and financial 
resources, research, environmental education, ecosystem 
conservation, population recovery, and consequently, a 
reduction in the risk of species extinction.
The Workshop for the Development of the Cavernas 
do Brasil NAP was held in Serra do Cipó/MG from 
November 23 to 25, 2021. It was coordinated by ICMBio/
Cecav and employed participatory planning methods 
and techniques outlined in the institutional guidelines, 
currently published in Normative Instruction ICMBio nº 
21/2018. The in-person workshop aimed to establish 
the general objectives, specific objectives, and actions of 
the NAP and was attended by 25 participants from 14 
institutions, including researchers, specialists, civil society 
organizations, and public institutions.
The NAP Planning Matrix includes objectives, actions, 
deliverables, deadlines, responsible parties, collaborators, 
estimated costs, geographic scope of each action, among 
other aspects. A Technical Advisory Group (GAT) was 
also established to assist in coordinating among involved 
actors, monitor, and evaluate the implementation of the 
Plan. A total of 44 actions were defined, distributed across 
four specific objectives, aimed at fulfilling the overarching 
goal. The Cavernas do Brasil NAP was formalized through 
ICMBio Ordinance nº 646/2022, and the GAT was 
established by ICMBio Ordinance nº 645/2022.

Strategy for the Conservation of Brazilian 
Speleological Heritage
The National Program for the Conservation 
of Threatened Species (Pró-Espécies), established 
by Ordinance nº 43/2014 of the Ministry of the 
Environment, sets forth the National Action Plans for the 
Conservation of Threatened Species (NAP). The primary 
purpose of the NAPs is to define actions aimed at the 
conservation and recovery of fauna species at risk of 
extinction. Additionally, Normative Instruction ICMBio 
nº 21/2018 provides guidelines for the development 
and implementation of these plans. NAPs are developed 
considering the main pressure vectors affecting the target 
species or environments and include objectives and 
actions established within a defined temporal horizon, 
with the goal of reversing or mitigating these threats.
The NAPs are prepared and implemented through a 
participatory process involving society, typically engaging 
specialists, public managers, organized civil society, 
representatives of productive sectors, and traditional 
communities, among other relevant stakeholders. This 
planning and management instrument has the potential 
to foster coordination among key social actors, as 
well as to guide the allocation of human and financial 
resources, research, environmental education, ecosystem 
conservation, population recovery, and consequently, a 
reduction in the risk of species extinction.
The Workshop for the Development of the Cavernas 
do Brasil NAP was held in Serra do Cipó/MG from 
November 23 to 25, 2021. It was coordinated by ICMBio/
Cecav and employed participatory planning methods 
and techniques outlined in the institutional guidelines, 
currently published in Normative Instruction ICMBio nº 
21/2018. The in-person workshop aimed to establish 
the general objectives, specific objectives, and actions of 
the NAP and was attended by 25 participants from 14 
institutions, including researchers, specialists, civil society 
organizations, and public institutions.
The NAP Planning Matrix includes objectives, actions, 
deliverables, deadlines, responsible parties, collaborators, 
estimated costs, geographic scope of each action, among 
other aspects. A Technical Advisory Group (GAT) was 
also established to assist in coordinating among involved 
actors, monitor, and evaluate the implementation of the 
Plan. A total of 44 actions were defined, distributed across 
four specific objectives, aimed at fulfilling the overarching 
goal. The Cavernas do Brasil NAP was formalized through 
ICMBio Ordinance nº 646/2022, and the GAT was 
established by ICMBio Ordinance nº 645/2022.
